title: The palace mourns
hook: Yasodhara's lament: why did he leave without me? (Buddhacarita 8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the penance grove, and your line: not through pain. Did you ask what one hardship was buying you? Today the poem turns around and goes home. Day seven hundred nine.

An empty saddle. That's what the city sees first. Kanthaka comes back through the gate with no rider, and Chandaka walks beside him holding a bundle of jewels. People run into the streets, looking past the horse for the prince, and he isn't there. The horse has come home. The rider hasn't. For a whole canto now, the poem leaves the hero in the forest and stays behind with everyone he left.
screen: `AN EMPTY SADDLE.` → `THE CITY RUNS OUT.` → `THE POEM STAYS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: First, the city. The poem fills the streets with weeping. The people had watched the prince ride out in splendor not long ago. Now the horse comes home without him, and the city feels like a house after a funeral. Second, the women of the palace, and Gautami, the queen who raised him after his mother died. She grieves over small, precise things, the way people do. In the poem she mourns his long, beautiful hair, now cut and lying somewhere on the forest floor. Third, Yashodhara, his wife. Her grief comes out as anger first, at Chandaka and even at the horse: why did you take him? Then it turns to the question underneath. In the poem, given here in paraphrase, she asks why he left without her. If he wanted the holy life, why not with her? She remembers the kings of old, his own ancestors in the stories, who went into the forest with their wives beside them. He has gone to seek the highest good, she says, and left his partner behind, as if the good were something to be won alone. She isn't asking him to stay a prince. She's asking why she had no part in the leaving. And fourth, the king. When Shuddhodana hears, the poem says, he falls to the ground in grief. All his walls, all his music, and the son is gone anyway. Here's what makes this canto matter. A story like this could skip this part. The hero walks out, and the camera follows him. Ashvaghosha keeps the camera in the palace and lets the grief speak in full. He doesn't argue with Yashodhara. He doesn't hurry her. The leaving was right for the prince, the poem believes, and it still cost someone. The one left behind.
screen: `A CITY IN MOURNING.` · `GAUTAMI GRIEVES HIS HAIR.` · `WHY DID HE LEAVE WITHOUT ME?` · `THE KING FALLS TO THE GROUND.` · then, large: `THE ONE LEFT BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor the one left behind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who was left behind by a choice. Maybe a choice you made: a parent when you moved away, a friend when your life went a different way. Maybe someone else's choice, and you were the one left. Let that person be in the room. Say their name inside. You don't need to undo anything, or decide who was right. Just let their side of the story have its say, the way the poem lets Yashodhara speak. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Yashodhara. The prince's wife, who asks in the poem why he left for the holy life without her, as the whole palace grieves his going. Today's word.
Your line: the one left behind. Today, reach out to one person who was left behind by a change in your life, even with a short message, and let them know they're remembered. Day seven hundred nine.

howItsDone: Yashodhara is remembered in Buddhist tradition, and in later tellings she becomes a nun herself; her lament is part of how some Buddhists reflect on the cost of the prince's leaving to those who loved him.

myth: in the poem, Yashodhara begs the prince to come back and rule
she asks why he left without her, not why he left the throne.
the poem stays in the palace for a whole canto after the leaving
it lets the grief of those left behind speak in full.
the poem scolds Yashodhara for her anger
it lets her speak without arguing back.

fork.setup: you're Yashodhara. the horse is home, the jewels are home, and your husband isn't. what do you do?
options: hide your grief and keep the palace calm.
speak your grief and your anger out loud.
set out after him into the forest.
fork.reveal: she speaks, first in anger at Chandaka and the horse, then asking why he left without her, when kings of old went to the forest with their wives.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of the prince's wife; Pali tellings often call her Yasodhara or Bimba.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story follows the prince, and his family just disappears.
what it means: the poem stops for a whole canto to hear the people he left, above all his wife.
what a scholar hears: Ashvaghosha gives Yashodhara a lament that appeals to the old royal custom of kings going to the forest with their wives.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 8 (the return of Chandaka and Kanthaka; the laments of the city, Gautami, Yashodhara and the king)

notes: All Buddhacarita material paraphrased (Cowell 1894 is not on the validator list).
Spelling: the outline has 'Yasodhara'; earlier days of this run use 'Yashodhara' (Sanskrit). Script keeps 'Yashodhara' for consistency; title and carry unchanged.

Confirm in Cowell canto 8: Gautami's lament over the cut hair; Yashodhara's reproach of Chandaka and Kanthaka; her appeal to ancestral kings who went to the forest with their wives; the king falling to the ground.
'The queen who raised him after his mother died': Maya's death is told in canto 2; confirm Gautami's role as stated.
howItsDone: Yashodhara's later ordination is from later tellings (e.g. the Therigatha commentary tradition); confirm, or cut the clause. 'Bimba' as a Pali name for her: confirm.
